- **Strengths:** Maximizes file system bandwidth for single time steps; effective when sending time is significant [S1].

The evidence explicitly states in Section 5.1 that using multiple input processors to read and preprocess a complete, single time step is advantageous to 'maximize bandwidth utilization of the parallel file system.' It further explains that this strategy is effective when the sending time ($T_s$) is significant relative to other times, as it allows the I/O and preprocessing costs to be hidden behind the rendering time, thereby maximizing efficiency for that specific time step.

The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states in Section 6 (Test Results) that 'the purpose of using 1DIP is to employ multiple input processors to fetch a single time step of the data for further cutting down the sending time, in contrast to 2DIP which concurrently reads multiple time steps.' This directly supports the claim that 1DIP focuses on parallelizing the read of one time step rather than concurrently reading multiple time steps. Furthermore, the text notes that this strategy reduces sending time to under 1 second, making it suitable when sending time is a bottleneck, which aligns with the second part of the claim.

- If $T_s$ becomes larger than $T_r$, 1DIP becomes less scalable compared to 2DIP [S1].

The claim states that if $T_s$ (send time) becomes larger than $T_r$ (rendering time), 1DIP becomes less scalable compared to 2DIP. Source [S1] explicitly states in Section 5.2: 'The strategy 1DIP works well until Ts become larger than Tr.' Furthermore, the Test Results section confirms that with 256 rendering processors, 'the 1DIP strategy is less scalable' because it cannot hide I/O/preprocessing costs as effectively as 2DIP (which uses m=14 to hide costs while 1DIP cannot). This aligns with the condition where high processor counts lead to increased send times ($T_s$) relative to rendering times ($T_r$), causing 1DIP to fail to hide overhead, thus being less scalable.

- Preprocessing cost can vary significantly; using simpler quantization methods can reduce $T_p$ substantially [S1].

The evidence explicitly states in the 'Test Results' section: 'The cost of preprocessing can vary significantly depending on the visualization requirements.' It further provides specific data: 'When we switched to a simple linear quantization method, the preprocessing cost was cut from 9.06 to 1.53 seconds.' This directly supports the claim that using simpler quantization methods can reduce preprocessing time ($T_p$) substantially.

- **Limitations:** Less scalable than 2DIP at high processor counts; requires careful tuning of $m$ [S1].

The claim states two limitations of the 1DIP strategy: 1) it requires careful tuning of $m$, and 2) it is less scalable than 2DIP at high processor counts. The evidence supports both points. First, the text explicitly provides formulas for calculating the optimal number of input processors $m$ ($m = (T_f + T_p)/T_s + 1$ or using $T_r$) to eliminate idle time or hide I/O costs, implying that $m$ must be determined based on specific timing parameters (tuning). Second, the text explicitly states in the test results section: 'our further tests using 256 rendering processors show that the 1DIP strategy is less scalable... using more than 14 input processors per group (i.e., m=14) with 2DIP, we can still completely hide the I/O and preprocessing cost, but not with IDIP.' This directly confirms the scalability comparison.
